label: GPT-6 Luna
output:
Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious about you becoming a maths teacher, I had to put it in writing. So here you are: a proper letter, delivered by post, like we’re in a period drama. I expect you to read it on the train and not just admire the envelope.

I know you’ve been doing quantity surveying in Croydon for nine years, and I know what “every day is the same spreadsheet” sounds like when you say it. You’ve been saying it for a while now. And on your birthday, when you said you wanted to do something that matters before 40, I thought: well, you could do a lot worse than teaching maths.

Before you start: I am not saying teaching is easy, noble, or a magical cure for being bored at work. It isn’t. The marking can feel endless. Behaviour can be wahala. Some days you’ll get home and want to speak to nobody, including me. I cried in the car park twice in my first term, back in 2019. I’m not hiding that from you, because you’d see through the sales pitch anyway. It does get better, though. You find your feet, your people, and the moments that make the hard bits feel worth it.

And, Kelechi, you would be good at it. Not because you got an A in Further Maths, although that certainly won’t hurt. Remember how you used to tutor half our hostel in Moremi before exams? You could explain something without making anyone feel stupid for not getting it straight away. You’re patient, funny, and you know how to make people feel at ease. Those are not small things in a classroom.

I still think about you helping my nephew with fractions at Christmas. You used portions of jollof rice on plates to explain them, and somehow he still talks about it. That’s teaching, isn’t it? Not standing at the front and performing expertise. Finding a way into someone’s head, using what they know, and helping the light come on.

I had one of those moments with a Year 11 boy in my class last month. Damola had been stuck on simultaneous equations for three weeks. Then it clicked. He looked at the page and shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped. I’m not going to pretend every lesson ends like a film, but every so often a young person surprises themselves, and you get to be there for it. That matters.

Our school in Peckham has 1,100 kids, and since September we’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups. There’s a real need for good teachers. I’m not telling you that to guilt-trip you into rescuing anyone. I’m telling you because you’d be doing something useful with what you already know—and because I can picture those kids liking you.

Yes, the pay would drop at first. I know that’s not a little detail, and I’m not going to wave it away with “but the holidays!” There’s a salaried training route where you’re paid while you train for a year, starting September 2027. You’d still need to look properly at the figures and decide whether the change works for you. There’s a pension, the holidays are better than yours, and pay rises over time, but none of that makes the first-year maths disappear. You should get the full picture before you make any decision.

And you’re 34, not 104. A woman in my department started at 41. You’re not too old to change direction. You’ve got years of checking other people’s costings ahead of you if you want them—but I can’t help thinking there’s more you could do with that sharp brain than stare at the same spreadsheet every day.

So here’s the actual ask: come with me to the open evening on Thursday 19 November at 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. Just come and listen, ask awkward questions, find out what the training and the job really involve. You do not have to sign anything, apply for anything, or dramatically announce a new calling. You can even spend the whole evening pretending you’re only there to keep me company.

Applications for next September open soon, so it’s worth finding out what’s on offer while there’s time. I’ll come with you. If you leave thinking it’s not for you, fine. I’ll buy you a drink and we’ll never speak of it again—unless you bring it up first, in which case I reserve the right to say “I told you so.”

You once said you wanted to do something that matters before 40. I’m not claiming teaching is the only way to do that. I am saying it might suit you more than another nine years of spreadsheets. And I’d like you to give the idea one evening before you dismiss it.

Bring questions. Bring your scepticism. Bring a jacket, because Lewisham in November will not care about your career plans.

See you on the 19th?

Your friend,

[Your name]
